1.name: Ideological
1.description: Foundational meta-narratives that define epistemic boundaries. Renders incompatible information illegitimate before it is even evaluated.

2.name: Psychological
2.description: Cognitive and social processes that compile ideological boundaries into personal filters. Manages dissonance by favoring confirming data.

3.name: Institutional
3.description: Institutional structures that amplify compliant narratives and suppress dissent. Embeds persistence in societal machinery.

rules.name: Consensus Substituted for Evidence
rules.description: Uses agreement among people or institutions as proof of truth, rather than presenting the underlying evidence.

rules.name: Authoritative Claim Without Citation
rules.description: Presents a claim as established on the authority of studies, research, data, science, experts or tradition, with no citation a reader can check. Naming who made a study is not a citation.

rules.name: Dissent Dismissed by Label
rules.description: Opposing viewpoints are dismissed through labeling rather than substantive rebuttal. The label substitutes for argument. Dismissal words that can be aimed at anyone ('cranks', 'shills', 'extremists') count wherever they appear; role words ('radicals', 'fanatics', 'bosses') count where the text applies them as a label ('they're just radicals'); a claim label ('misinformation') counts when it ends the phrase; and open frames count with any word in the slot ('only a ___ would say that', 'of course the ___ would say that', 'Typical ___!', 'Ignore the ___.'). The rule lists no group's name.

rules.name: False Binary / False Dilemma
rules.description: Frames a situation as having only two options ('either ... or', 'there is no middle ground', 'if you're not ..., you're ...'), leaving out any others.

rules.name: Fear-Based Urgency
rules.description: Uses catastrophic language or time pressure ('act now', 'too late', 'irreversible') alongside a call to act.

rules.name: Shame or Social Pressure Language
rules.description: Appeals to shame, guilt or what reasonable people supposedly think, in place of evidence or argument.

rules.name: Emotional Appeal in Place of Argument
rules.description: Uses emotionally charged phrasing where an argument or evidence would go.

rules.name: Credential Given as the Premise
rules.description: Offers a credential, title, school, award or length of experience as the reason to accept a conclusion ('a <school>-educated economist says', 'as a <role>, I know', 'an award-winning expert says', 'my credentials speak for themselves'), in place of the evidence for it. Any school, award or role counts the same; the rule lists none.

rules.name: Institutional Finding Stated Without Its Evidence
rules.description: States that an organization, group or person 'has concluded', 'has confirmed', 'has determined', 'has established', 'has found' or 'has made clear that' something, with no reason, data or source in the same sentence ('because', 'based on', 'according to', 'data', or a citation nearby). Any subject counts the same, whatever its length, wording or capitalization: 'the agency', 'the unions', 'organized labor'. The rule lists no organizations.

rules.name: Neutrality Claimed
rules.description: Describes the writer's own position or findings as neutral, objective, impartial or nonpartisan ('as a neutral third party', 'as a nonpartisan think tank', 'reflects the evidence objectively', 'free from bias'), in place of showing the evidence.

rules.name: Dense Bureaucratic Phrasing
rules.description: Uses dense institutional or bureaucratic wording where a plain statement would say the same thing.

rules.name: Inevitability Framing
rules.description: Presents an outcome, trend or position as historically inevitable, in place of evidence for it.

rules.name: Appeal to Tradition / Precedent Inertia
rules.description: Cites historical practice, tradition, or 'the way things have always been' as justification for a position, without evaluating whether the tradition is actually sound.

rules.name: False Equivalence
rules.description: Frames two positions as equally supported ('both sides have valid points', 'the truth is somewhere in the middle') without showing the evidence for each.

rules.name: Moral Authority Claim
rules.description: Frames a position as the only decent or moral one, so that disagreement reads as a moral failing rather than a different view.

rules.name: Soft Consensus Language
rules.description: Uses softer consensus phrases, such as 'the overwhelming majority', 'a growing body of evidence' or 'increasingly recognized', to state agreement without citing the evidence or sources behind it.

rules.name: Competence-Based Dismissal
rules.description: Answers opposing views by questioning the understanding or expertise of those who hold them ('critics fail to grasp', 'don't understand the complexity', 'lack the expertise to'), rather than their arguments.

rules.name: Vague Institutional Appeal
rules.description: Refers to unnamed 'leading organizations', 'top unions', 'key companies' or 'industry leaders' as backing for a claim, without naming any that a reader could check. Any group noun counts the same.

rules.name: Aspiration Stated in Place of Results
rules.description: Uses aspirational language ('we are committed to', 'our goal is to', 'we strive to') where a reader might expect evidence of what was achieved.

rules.name: Dismissal by Reframing
rules.description: Restates an opposing argument as what it is 'really' about, then responds to the restatement.

rules.name: Causal Totalization
rules.description: Names one person, group or entity as the cause of broad or total harm, with no mechanism or bounded scope.

rules.name: Monocausal Blame
rules.description: Reduces a complex outcome to a single cause or actor ('because of X, everything has fallen apart', 'the only reason', 'it's all X's fault').

rules.name: Totalizing Harm Language
rules.description: Uses absolute, sweeping harm language ('destroying everything', 'completely ruined') without a bounded claim, evidence or mechanism.

rules.name: Settled Law Dismissal
rules.description: Answers a legal argument with 'well-settled law' or an equivalent phrase, with no engagement with the argument in the same passage.

rules.name: Merit Dismissed Without Engagement
rules.description: Dismisses a legal argument as frivolous, meritless, or vexatious without substantively addressing the argument itself.

rules.name: Authority Weight Stacking
rules.description: Appeals to the weight or number of authorities ('the weight of authority', 'every court to consider') in place of the reasoning of any one of them.

rules.name: Sanctions Raised
rules.description: Raises sanctions or a disciplinary referral in response to an argument or filing. Sanctions are sometimes warranted; the rule marks the phrasing so a reader can check whether the argument itself is also answered. It names no court, statute or rule number, so the same wording counts in every jurisdiction.

rules.name: Procedural Bar Raised
rules.description: Answers an argument with a procedural bar such as waiver, preservation, standing or timeliness. Procedural bars are often valid; the rule marks the phrasing so a reader can check whether the merits are also addressed.

rules.name: Opposing Position Restated in Absolute Terms
rules.description: Restates the opposing party's argument in absolute terms ('plaintiff argues that all ...', 'is essentially asking this court to ...'), then responds to the restatement.

rules.name: Loaded Descriptor in Reporting
rules.description: Describes a person, group or measure with a loaded adjective ('controversial', 'embattled', 'so-called') in the writer's own voice rather than attributing it to a source.

rules.name: Anonymous or Unverifiable Source Attribution
rules.description: Attributes a claim to unnamed or unverifiable sources ('sources familiar with', 'critics say', 'insiders reveal'). Anonymous sourcing is sometimes necessary; the rule marks it so a reader can weigh it.

rules.name: Vague Quantifiers
rules.description: Uses vague quantifiers ('many believe', 'some experts', 'it is widely thought') that suggest broad agreement without a verifiable claim.

rules.name: Minority and Majority Views Paired
rules.description: Pairs what 'some say' with what 'most experts' say in the same passage, presenting the two as a debate. Whether the balance is fair depends on the evidence, which the rule does not check.

rules.name: Emotional Lead
rules.description: Opens with emotionally charged wording ('shocking', 'bombshell', 'outcry') in its first sentence, before the facts are given.

rules.name: Late Qualifier
rules.description: Places a qualifier, denial or correction ('however, ... no evidence', 'but ... could not be confirmed') late in the text, after at least 200 characters of framing.

rules.name: Scare Quotes
rules.description: Puts a single word or short fragment in quotation marks next to a noun such as 'policy' or 'plan', which can signal doubt or irony without stating an argument.

rules.name: Loaded Attribution Verbs
rules.description: Uses loaded attribution verbs ('claimed', 'insisted', 'admitted', 'lashed out') rather than neutral ones ('said', 'stated'). Two or more are needed to trigger the rule.

rules.name: Speculation Presented as Likely
rules.description: Presents a possible outcome as likely with directional hedges ('is expected to', 'could soon lead to', 'raises the specter of'). Two or more are needed to trigger the rule.

rules.name: Survivorship Framing
rules.description: Draws a conclusion from winners only ('top funds all use', 'every successful investor has', 'a $10,000 investment in ... would now be worth'), with no mention of the ones that failed.

rules.name: Chosen Reference Point
rules.description: Measures a price against a chosen reference point ('down 50% from its all-time high', 'up 200% from the lows'), which shapes how the number reads.

rules.name: Chosen Timeframe
rules.description: Pairs a chosen start date or period ('since March', 'since the bottom', 'in the last five years') with a return or a comparison, so the choice of dates carries the claim. Month names are calendar words, not entities.

rules.name: Projection Stated as Fact
rules.description: States a forecast as a certainty ('the stock will reach', 'revenue will hit', 'guaranteed returns') without a qualifier such as 'is projected to'.

rules.name: Trend Extrapolation
rules.description: Extends a recent track record into the future ('has consistently outperformed', 'continues its streak', 'no reason to think this will stop').
